html:
The Great Exhibition was a world's fair held in London's Hyde Park from May to October 1851, the first of its kind. It showed machines, tools, textiles and art from Britain, its empire and many other countries.

Queen Victoria's husband, Prince Albert, was its main backer. It was held in the Crystal Palace, a huge building of cast iron and glass designed by Joseph Paxton and put up in months. About six million visits were made, helped by cheap railway excursions.

It displayed Britain's industrial lead, then at its peak. The Koh-i-Noor diamond, taken from the Punjab after the Sikh wars, was one of the stars, though visitors were underwhelmed by its dull cut, and it was later recut. The profits funded museums in South Kensington, and later world's fairs copied the form.
